title: Degraded performance in versions `>=1.1.412`, worse with multiple threads
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
We have a monorepo where we use `pyright` in CI to ensure proper typing. Up to version `1.1.411` using 8 threads it would take ~1 minute to run `pyright` on our codebase (~5K python files). Starting in `1.1.412` it takes ~22m.

**Code or Screenshots**
Testing with following script:
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for THREADS in 1 8
do
    for VERSION in 410 411 412 413 414
    do
        pnpm add -D "pyright@1.1.$VERSION" --no-optional 2>&1
        ./node_modules/.bin/pyright --version 1>&2
        time ./node_modules/.bin/pyright --threads $THREADS src/ 1>pyright.t$THREADS.v1.1.$VERSION.out 2>pyright.t$THREADS.v1.1.$VERSION.err
    done
done
```

With `THREADS=1`, it goes from ~3.5 minutes to 45 minutes:
Version | Real | User | Sys
-- | -- | -- | --
pyright 1.1.410 | 3m37.992s | 5m41.581s | 0m12.607s
pyright 1.1.411 | 3m38.553s | 5m39.328s | 0m11.544s
pyright 1.1.412 | 15m53.537s | 20m19.392s | 0m19.188s
pyright 1.1.413 | 55m29.642s | 60m10.076s | 0m37.799s
pyright 1.1.414 | 44m14.298s | 24m42.466s | 0m59.330s

With `THREADS=8`, it goes  from ~1 to ~22 minutes:
Version | Real | User | Sys
-- | -- | -- | --
pyright 1.1.410 | 1m4.128s | 9m0.630s | 0m57.164s
pyright 1.1.411 | 1m0.468s | 8m42.691s | 0m44.016s
pyright 1.1.412 | 22m10.466s | 31m45.013s | 0m55.151s
pyright 1.1.413 | 22m27.549s | 32m52.530s | 1m16.357s
pyright 1.1.414 | 22m14.179s | 32m37.119s | 1m31.261s

As an added insight, with versions `>=412`, when using multiple threads the first `N-1` workers finish as quickly as in versions `<=411`, and the last worker lingers at 100% CPU for the remainder of the time.

title: Function redefinition is flagged if the types are generic
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
Conditionally defining a function two different ways is reported as a redeclaration if the types are generic, but not if the types are definite.

**Code or Screenshots**

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import ParamSpec, TypeVar

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")

try:
    import coverage  # pyright: ignore[reportUnusedImport]
except ImportError:

    def f(a: str) -> int:
        return 1

    def fgen(func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
        return func
else:

    def f(a: str) -> int:
        return 2

    def fgen(func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
        return func
```

Running with 1.1.413, I get:
```
% pyright /tmp/bug.py
/tmp/bug.py
  /tmp/bug.py:21:9 - error: Function declaration "fgen" is obscured by a declaration of the same name (reportRedeclaration)
1 error, 0 warnings, 0 informations
```

`f` is fine to redefine, but `fgen` is considered a problem.  Both are the same: the name has the same type under either condition.

title: Publish the documented pyright-typeserver package to npm
body_truncated:
### Description

[This Pyright Type Server doc](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/docs/type-server.md) says: 
>  It is distributed as a separate npm package, pyright-typeserver, and is exposed through the pyright-typeserver executable.

But there is no `pyright-typeserver` package published to `npm`. 

Pyright contains `packages/pyright-typeserver` and documents the Type Server as a separately distributed `npm` package. The documented command is:

```text
pyright-typeserver --stdio
```

However, the current release pipeline packages only `packages/pyright`. It does not package or publish `packages/pyright-typeserver`. Registry lookup therefore returns “package not found,” while the published pyright package exposes only `pyright` and `pyright-langserver`

### Evidence
- [Type Server documentation](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/docs/type-server.md)
- [Type Server package manifest](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/packages/pyright-typeserver/package.json)
- [Pyright release pipeline](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/build/azuredevops/azure-pipelines-release.yml)
- [PR #11537: Add standalone Type Server Protocol server](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/pull/11537)
- [PR #11625: Align pyright-typeserver version with Pyright](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/pull/11625)

### Request

Please publish `pyright-typeserver` to `npm` for each Pyright release that includes the Type Server.
Please keep the `pyright` and `pyright-typeserver` versions aligned and add the Type Server package to the standard release pipeline.
If public npm publication is not intended, please update the documentation with the supported distribution and installation path.

### Use case
Agent and code-generation tools need direct access to inferred, declared, and expected Python types through TSP. Consumers also need an official, versioned artifact that can be locked and mirrored through enterprise npm proxies.

title: Signature of dataclass __init__ inferred incorrectly, when overriding a field with a default without specifying a new default
body_truncated:
**Bug description:**
When overriding a dataclass field (say `x`) with a default, with a field without a default as follows: `x: int = field()`, the `__init__` signature doesn't contain a default value for `x` at runtime. But pyright's inferred signature does contain a default.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Base:
    x: int = 1  # Field with a default

@dataclass
class Foo(Base):
    x: int = field()  # This line shouldn't be marked as an error (unless it causes a default arg to appear after a non-default arg). Pyright does mark it as an error.

Foo()  # This line should be marked as an error. Pyright doesn't
```

**More info:**

The runtime behavior of stdlib dataclasses when field with defaults are overridden without specifying a new default is kinda complicated and depends on the specific form of the override.
1. When the form is `x: int = field()` (as in the code snippet above):
    (a) Remove default value of `x` from `Foo.__init__`.
    (b) Subclasses of `Foo` can still inherit the default value of `x` defined in `Base`.
2. When the form is `x: int`:
    (a) Keep the default value of `x` from `Base` in `Foo.__init__`.
    (b) Subclasses of `Foo` can still inherit  the default value of `x` defined in `Base`.
3. When the form is `x: int = field(init=False)`:
    (a) Remove the parameter `x` from `Foo.__init__`.
    (b) Subclasses of `Foo` can still inherit the default value of `x` defined in `Base`.

Pyright handles the `x: int = field()` and `x: int` forms identically, matching the runtime behavior of the `x: int` form. OTOH, mypy, ty, and pyrefly handle the `x: int = field()` and `x: int` forms identically, matching the runtime behavior of the `x: int = field()` form.

For my purposes (which involves a custom dataclass mechanism), I only care that the `x: int = field()` form is handled properly (I forbid the `x: int` form via runtime checks). I'd really appreciate it if the narrower bug described near the top is fixed.

*

title: Regression in 1.1.411: match loses some of the context
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
After upgrading from 1.1.410 to 1.1.411 a piece of pattern matching code based on generics that had previously typechecked without issues, started failing. It looks like if the typer now uses an upper bound instead of a specific, already determined type. If I were to guess, this seems to be related to #11489.

**Code**

Python 3.14

```python
class Wrapper[A: str | list]:
    data: A

# This is fine:
def successful_direct(obj: Wrapper[list]) -> list:
    return obj.data
    
# This is fine too:
def successful_isinstance(obj: Wrapper[list]) -> list:
    if isinstance(obj, Wrapper):
        return obj.data

# This fails with: Type "str | list[Unknown]" is not assignable to return type "list[Unknown]"
def failing_match_unpack(obj: Wrapper[list]) -> list:
    match obj:
        case Wrapper(data=data):
            return data

# This also fails with: Type "str | list[Unknown]" is not assignable to return type "list[Unknown]"
def failing_match_instance_type_check(obj: Wrapper[list]) -> list:
    match obj:
        case Wrapper():
            return obj.data

```

**Interesting observations** (to help pinpoint the issue):
- If I replace the generic `list` with a specific 1st order type like `int`, everything **typechecks** correctly.
- If I specify the exact `list` type, e.g. `list[int]` instead of bare `list`, it **typechecks** correctly.
- If I spell out the open list type explicitly, i.e. use `list[Any]` instead of `list`, it **fails** in the same way as above.
- If I replace the list with some other higher-order generic like `dict`, `set` or a custom `Container`, it **fails** in the same way.

**VS Code extension or command-line**
Fails on: CLI, 1.1.411
Last worked on: CLI, 1.1.410

title: Closed TypedDicts losing type discrimination
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
Adding `closed=True` to a TypedDict appears to be disabling type discrimination.

This is related to, but kind of the opposite of, #10805: in that case, unsafe discrimination for open `TypedDict`s is being allowed as it is idiomatic; in this case, *safe* discrimination for closed `TypedDict`s is being disallowed.

In the example below, `Bar` is closed so cannot contain a `"foo"` key; `"foo" in u` should therefore narrow the type of `u` to `Foo`, but this is not happening.

**Code or Screenshots**
```python
from typing import TypedDict

class Foo(TypedDict, closed=True):
    foo: int

class Bar(TypedDict, closed=True):  # Removing "closed" here causes the error to go away
    bar: int

U = Foo | Bar

def get_field(u: U) -> int:
    if "foo" in u:
        return u["foo"]  # E: "foo" is not a defined key in "Bar"
    else:
        return u["bar"]
```

title: Pyright is incorrectly handling overload functions
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

According to the [official Python spec for overload](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/overload.html), the `@overload` function can be followed by a single non-overload function:

> In regular modules, a series of `@overload`-decorated definitions must be followed by exactly one non-`@overload`-decorated definition (for the same function/method).
>
> The `@overload`-decorated definitions are for the benefit of the type checker only, since they will be overwritten by the non-`@overload`-decorated definition, while the latter is used at runtime but ***should be ignored by a type checker***.

The spec also gives an example of an overloaded function, which does not specify types for the non-overloaded function:

```python
@overload
def utf8(value: None) -> None:
    pass
@overload
def utf8(value: bytes) -> bytes:
    pass
@overload
def utf8(value: unicode) -> bytes:
    pass
def utf8(value):
    <actual implementation>
```

class Foo:

In order to suppress those errors, I need to add an `int | str` union type to the final non-overload function.

In that simple example it might seem okay, but with complicated types it can be very tricky indeed. Here is a real example from my project:

title: KW_ONLY is only recognized when assigned to _
body_truncated:
### **Description**
When creating a `KW_ONLY` field in a dataclass, the typical convention is to attach it to `_`. However, as Python documentation states, _[this is simply a convention](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html#dataclasses.KW_ONLY)_, and the name is ignored regardless. At runtime, the field effectively doesn't exist.

However, Pyright will not recognize it under anything else, as the `KW_ONLY` check is locked behind a field specifically being `_`. This goes against official Python behavior and documentation.

https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/63998f4d0720a86447f4c4a04716e34f3e703660/packages/pyright-internal/src/analyzer/dataClasses.ts#L378-L388

As such, it will not recognize which fields should be keyword-only. In some cases, Pyright will not report anything, making the issue invisible. However, it will raise an false positive if `KW_ONLY` is after fields with defaults, as seen below.

### **Code example**

The real world example that inspired this issue. Another common convention with `_` is to assign [`gettext`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/gettext.html#gettext.gettext) to it. However, when assigning translatable text into a dataclass field's default, it will conflict with `_: KW_ONLY`, as now `_` has been reassigned (to nothing) in the class scope.

The simplest solution, which seems to generally satisfy linters, is to assign `KW_ONLY` to `__` instead. However, Pyright will complain about this too, stating "Fields without default values cannot appear after fields with default values". This error is reported as simply "`reportGeneralTypeIssues`", meaning it cannot be selectively silenced. Any call to the class constructor will also now be flagged, as Pyright believes there is a required (ironically positional) argument that is missing.

The issue can currently be silenced by assigning `field(default_factory=KW_ONLY)` to the `KW_ONLY` typed field, but this is rather abnormal and not very Pythonic.

title: False negative for callable assignability
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

Pyright reports a false negative when checking assignability between two callable types when the RHS has variadic and keyword-variadic parameters while the LHS has only standard parameter. Refer to the code example below.

**Code or Screenshots**

```python
from typing import Protocol


class A(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, *args: int, **kwargs: bool) -> None: ...


class B(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, a: int) -> None: ...


def _(a: A):
    # This should be not assignable
    x: B = a
```

The reason is that the positional form of the standard parameter is matched against the variadic parameter and is assignable but the keyword form of the standard parameter is not assignable to kwargs because `int` is not assignable to `bool`.

Here, `x(a=10)` is not a valid call as the type of keyword-variadic is a `bool`.

mypy does report this as an error:
```
mypy: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "A", variable has type "B") 
    Following member(s) of "A" have conflicts:
        Expected:
            def __call__(self, a: int) -> None
        Got:
            def __call__(self, *args: int, **kwargs: bool) -> None [assignment]
```

**VS Code extension or command-line**

Command-line with version `1.1.398`

title: Import resolution not respecting virtual environments
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

When updating from `1.1.321` to `1.1.327`, I am receiving `reportMissingImports` in all of my projects. I use poetry to manage python dependencies & virtual environment for both local deployment and pipeline execution.

> **EDIT:** Tested with `1.1.326` and this bug is not present so it was introduced in `1.1.327`

When running pyright, I run `npm exec --no -- pyright --venvpath ./` with `venv = ".venv"` set in my `pyproject.toml`. I typically (especially in pipeline executions) do not activate the virtual environment prior to running pyright.

For all versions prior to `1.1.327`, this worked fine. However, after updating pyright raises `reportMissingImports` for all dependencies that exist only in my virtual environment (e.g. `pytest` for my tests).

title: `BufferedWriter` is not compatible with `SupportsWrite[AnyStr]`
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
Sorry for the rambling title – I couldn't think of a good description of this:

```python
import shutil
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, AnyStr
from io import BufferedWriter

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from _typeshed import SupportsRead, SupportsWrite


def f(s: SupportsRead[AnyStr], t: SupportsWrite[AnyStr]) -> None:  # with TypeVar
    shutil.copyfileobj(s, t)


def g(s: SupportsRead[bytes], t: SupportsWrite[bytes]) -> None:  # with concrete type
    shutil.copyfileobj(s, t)


def h(src: SupportsRead[bytes], tgt: BufferedWriter) -> None:
    f(src, tgt)  # E: Argument of type "BufferedWriter" cannot be assigned to parameter "t" of type "SupportsWrite[AnyStr@f]" in function "f"
    g(src, tgt)
```

**Expected behavior**
If I can pass `tgt` succesfully to `g`, then I don't see why it would fail with `f`. Clearly, `BufferedWriter` is compatible with `SupportsWrite[bytes]`.

**VS Code extension or command-line**
command-line

**Additional context**
This happened after updating to the most recent version. I believe there were typeshed changes around this code.

title: Pyright with venv still uses Python 2.7 on MacOS
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
The (unsupported) python2.7 interpreter bundled with MacOS is still chosen by pyright (despite the fixes in #829), but only when a venv is specified.

**To Reproduce**
Specify a "venvPath" and "venv" in config.  Start `pyright --verbose" in that directory:

```
  Python version 2.7 from interpreter is unsupported
```

**Expected behavior**
pyright checks for python3 and finds it in the venv (even `python` in the venv points to python3).

**Additional context**
It appears the fallback python3 -> python is disabled in the presence of a venv, _and_ the venv is not first activated when determining the interpreter.

title: Incorrect handling of client-initiatied progress
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
I believe that in this code:

https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/b12f1347b2b3fbfdb1da68583e35226817f7de7b/packages/pyright-internal/src/languageServerBase.ts#L462-L467

the `params.workDoneToken` will always be `undefined` since the LSP library will remove the property in

https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-languageserver-node/blob/859a8ece3e14b130d531c6102b2d108196436bc4/server/src/common/progress.ts#L139-L147

called from:

https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-languageserver-node/blob/859a8ece3e14b130d531c6102b2d108196436bc4/server/src/common/server.ts#L1696-L1698

and pass it through the `workDoneReporter` argument in the pyright handler function.

So the server is never using the client-initiated progress token but always creating server-initiated one.

title: Cannot access members of class in with statement
body_truncated:
Hi,

Just installed pyright for coc-nvim yesterday and ran into a weird error when editing some old code. If there's something I missed I'll be happy to provide more info.

**Describe the bug**
The bug is that pyright cannot access members of my class when used in a with statement. Outside of a with statement it detects them correctly (jump to definition and all that works). The class i have inherits from requests.Session and it seems to me that pyright does detect all methods related to requests.Session but none from my own class. So my assumption is that pyright incorrectly believes the type is requests.Session instead of my own.

The error message i recieve for the code below is:
[Pyright reportGeneralTypeIssues] [E] Cannot access member "some_method" for type "Session"

As i added the above I realised that it even says the type is Session when it in fact should be Test. My real code uses the name Session so I did not realise this before.

**To Reproduce**
Write a small class inheriting from requests.Session and add a new method. Then create an instance of this session with the with statement and try to access the method you added.

This code is what I created to reproduce the results. Unfortunately i cannot share the real code.

test.some_method()  # No error message

with Test("aString") as session:

title: PEP 563 should not be enabled by default in Python 3.10
body_truncated:
It was recently decided that PEP 563 behavior would _not_ be enabled by default in Python 3.10. (See [this thread](https://mail.python.org/archives/list/python-dev@python.org/thread/CLVXXPQ2T2LQ5MP2Y53VVQFCXYWQJHKZ/) for details.)

Pyright currently assumes that this behavior will be enabled by default when configured for use with Python 3.10.
